documents: Mejia et al. 2022, Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2022GL100058 (published paper, PDF, 10 pages)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (n of 10), identical to PDF pages counted from 1

entry.evidence: Links between hydrology and sliding of the Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS) are poorly understood.

steps.action: The authors pose the question of how moulin distribution and the timing of meltwater delivery to moulins affect sliding, which they say is under-investigated.
steps.quote: how the spatial distribution of moulins and differences in the timing of meltwater delivery to moulins impact sliding has not been fully investigated

steps.action: From published work, they take up the expectation that melt-sliding lags arise from longer meltwater delivery delays in larger catchments, which grow with elevation as moulin density falls.
steps.quote: These lags are likely caused by longer delays in the timing of meltwater delivery to moulins with larger catchment areas

steps.action: They design a paired-site campaign: two camps at different elevations, each with one internally drained catchment, to time daily peaks in melt, moulin input, moulin head and ice velocity.
steps.quote: We established two field camps at different elevations

steps.action: They deploy instruments in the 2017 and 2018 melt seasons: weather stations, ultrasonic stream-stage sensors, moulin pressure transducers, GNSS stations, a seismic station, and gauges on two auxiliary catchments.
steps.quote: We measured moulin water level by directly instrumenting moulins with pressure transducers

steps.action: They calculate melt rates from the weather data with an enhanced temperature-index model to time peak meltwater production (about 13:30 local time).
steps.quote: the enhanced temperature-index model by Pellicciotti et al. (2005) to calculate melt rates

steps.action: They check modeled melt timing against measured surface ablation at Low Camp, and against both camps over two seasons, then adopt a single melt timeseries.
steps.quote: A comparison between calculated melt rate and ice surface ablation recorded at Low Camp

steps.action: They compare delivery lags against catchment area, length, elongation and slope; area controls most strongly (JEME 2.4 h vs RADI 6.5 h); data are restricted to bare-ice conditions.
steps.quote: catchment area exerted the strongest controls on the timing of peak meltwater delivery to moulins

steps.action: They test the lag-area relation on two independent auxiliary catchments (JNIH 1.1 km2, SBPI 2.4 km2), which confirm it.
steps.quote: Observations from our two auxiliary catchments confirm the pattern of longer lags

steps.action: They compare moulin head timeseries at the two sites: the delivery-to-head lag is about 2 h at both, and RADI head peaks 1-3.25 h later in the day than JEME.
steps.quote: The lag between peak meltwater delivery to moulins and peak moulin head was similar, approximately 2 hr, at both sites

steps.action: They relate peak moulin head to peak sliding: the two coincide at Low Camp (r = 0.86), while at High Camp sliding lags head by about 2.8-3.0 h.
steps.quote: We find a strong agreement between the timing of peak moulin head and peak sliding speed at Low Camp

steps.action: They replicate the Low Camp head-sliding coincidence across 2017 (JEME) and 2018 (PIRA), and the High Camp lag across two GNSS stations (EORM, HMID).
steps.quote: This pattern was observed during 2017 and 2018

steps.action: They check the seismic tremor proxy against stream stage: peak meltwater delivery to PIRA coincides with peak tremor amplitude.
steps.quote: Peak meltwater delivery to PIRA moulin coincided with peak tremor amplitude

steps.action: They use 2018 tremor amplitude to track seasonal change; the tremor lag behind melt falls from 6.1 h in June to 3.5 h in July and 1.4 h in August.
steps.quote: tremor amplitude peaked earlier in the day as the melt season progressed

steps.action: They check the tremor-derived seasonal shift against the independent stream-stage record, which shows a 54-minute drop in lag between July and August.
steps.quote: These observations agree with stream stage measurements

steps.action: They set the lag-area relation against unit-hydrograph expectations and published supraglacial catchment studies (Smith et al. 2017): even a narrow area range gives delivery differences of over 4 h.
steps.quote: Our observations show that even a more limited range of catchment sizes

steps.action: They explain the seasonal shift by early-season snow cover followed by increasing drainage density, and compare the snow effect with Willis et al. (2002).
steps.quote: snow cover was likely responsible for the longer residence time of meltwater within the supraglacial drainage system

steps.action: They retain an inherent 2 h delay between peak delivery and peak moulin head, against the earlier assumption that the two peaks are simultaneous.
steps.quote: This contrasts previous assumptions that peak meltwater delivery to moulins and peak moulin head would occur simultaneously

steps.action: They compare melt-sliding lags with Hoffman et al. (2011) and conclude that moulin head timing only partly accounts for the later sliding peak at High Camp.
steps.quote: the timing of peak moulin head was only partially responsible for the later timing of peak sliding

steps.action: They propose that low moulin density at High Camp makes sliding depend on pressure migrating from a single conduit into the distributed system.
steps.quote: sliding will be more coupled to the pressure change emanating from an individual conduit as it migrates into the distributed system

steps.action: They take from Werder et al. (2013) the model expectation that single-conduit pressurization spreads up to 2 km with a phase lag of up to 6 h.
steps.quote: the diurnal pressurization of a single conduit can extend up to 2 km into the distributed system

steps.action: They keep finite pressure diffusion from the single conduit as a plausible explanation of the 2 h head-to-sliding lag at High Camp.
steps.quote: In this paradigm, the finite diffusion speed of the pressure change within the conduit at the base of High Camp's primary moulin could produce

steps.action: They restrict the alpine-glacier head-sliding coupling (Iken 1972) to high-moulin-density, lower-elevation areas and say it breaks down inland.
steps.quote: the straightforward coupling between effective pressure and ice motion derived from studies on alpine glaciers breaks down for inland reaches

steps.action: They conclude that the supraglacial drainage system controls hydrodynamic coupling through routing delays and through the spatial distribution of moulins.
steps.quote: the supraglacial drainage system controls hydrodynamic coupling by two mechanisms

tree.answer: Diurnal lag cascade from melt through moulin input and moulin head to sliding, differing with elevation
Yes for stream stage, moulin head and velocity; melt is modeled
Explain how catchment properties and moulin density set the timing of pressurization and sliding
Implicit only: coincident-delivery assumption vs catchment routing delay; for the sliding lag, only the moulin-density/pressure-diffusion account
Not formally derived; the coincidence assumption implies zero lag, which is measured against
Conditions found in nature at two elevations during live melt seasons

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Yes: many daily cycles, four catchments, two seasons
Survives auxiliary catchments, a second year, a second GNSS station and an independent tremor record
Kept: moulin density likely explains the delayed sliding peak at High Camp

end.claim: Larger, higher-elevation catchments delay peak moulin head, and low moulin density at higher elevations likely makes peak sliding lag peak moulin head by about 2.8 h, so moulin density controls the timing of peak pressurization and its coupling to sliding.

decisive_move.sentence: Co-located direct measurements of stream stage, moulin head and GNSS velocity in catchments at two elevations produced the full lag cascade; without them neither the phase shift nor the head-sliding offset exists.

gates.evidence: The two-elevation design follows the cited expectation that delays grow with catchment area and elevation (p. 2). The lag-area relation was tested on independent auxiliary catchments and could have failed (p. 6). The moulin-density mechanism is offered post hoc with a cited model and is not tested (p. 8). Nothing was fixed before the data were collected.

imports.item: kernel density estimates and box plots (violin plots) for the distributions of peak timing
ultrasonic water level sensors and pressure transducers

novelty_claims.quote: [...] a novel and holistic approach to understanding relationships between melting and sliding on the GrIS
we take the novel approach of monitoring meltwater's propagation through the entire glacial hydraulic system at two elevations

limits: No peer-review file was supplied; the acknowledgments say two reviewers improved the manuscript, but what changed is unknown. The Supporting Information was not supplied, so checks described only in Texts S2-S9 and Figures S7-S17 are coded from main-text mentions. Sub-claim statuses: (a) delivery lag increases with catchment area is regularity_in_range (four catchments, 0.2-16.8 km2, r = 0.67); (b) a 2 h delivery-to-head lag and a 2.8-3.0 h head-to-sliding lag at High Camp are estimate_with_resolution (stated ±1 sigma); (c) the seasonal shift explained by snow cover and drainage density is best_explanation, inferred and not tested. The moulin-density mechanism is supported only by reasoning from the cited Werder et al. (2013) model, not by a test that could fail (inference). Moulin head was measured at only two sites, so elevation, catchment area and moulin density are confounded, as the authors note in the Conclusions. Melt is modeled, not measured, except for the ablation check. Composition choice: natures_repetition fits the repeated diurnal cycles and the fitted lag relations, but the headline mechanism has trace_series-like best_explanation status; coder judgment. Moulin-density values come from Figures S4-S5, not seen.

disagreements.target: McGrath et al. (2011) and the assumption that peak meltwater delivery and peak moulin head are simultaneous
disagreements.support: Direct moulin head and stream-stage measurements show a consistent ~2 h lag at both sites and across the season.
disagreements.quote: This contrasts previous assumptions that peak meltwater delivery to moulins and peak moulin head would occur simultaneously (e.g., McGrath et al., 2011).

disagreements.target: Common assumption that meltwater reaches the bed coincident with peak melting across the ablation area
disagreements.support: Measured delivery lags of 2.4-6.5 h that increase with catchment area.
disagreements.quote: [...] supraglacial drainage system is overlooked under the assumption that meltwater delivery to the subglacial drainage system is coincident with peak melting

disagreements.target: Alpine glaciers as analogs for the GrIS (head-sliding correlation, Iken 1972)
disagreements.support: The head-sliding coincidence holds at Low Camp (r = 0.86) but not at High Camp (r = 0.46), where moulin density is low.
disagreements.quote: the straightforward coupling between effective pressure and ice motion derived from studies on alpine glaciers breaks down for inland reaches

alternatives_considered.chosen: catchment area as the controlling characteristic
alternatives_considered.alternatives: catchment length, elongation ratio, average surface slope
alternatives_considered.reason: strongest correlation; length correlates mainly because it covaries with area (r = 0.996)

alternatives_considered.chosen: a single timeseries of peak melting for all sites
alternatives_considered.reason: similarity in observations between weather stations

alternatives_considered.chosen: exclude velocity spikes from rainfall and the lake drainage event
use only bare-ice data for primary catchment delivery timing
alternatives_considered.reason: eliminates the influence of the seasonal snowpack
